How this register works

Decision register: built; 16 decisions to make (9 plan decisions, 5 manual actions, 2 plan statements, 2 of them with the draft's DEFAULT to confirm or change) · 1 default to confirm (other records than the 2 with the draft's DEFAULT, no step waits for them: 3 default records in all) · 50 units to review (310 critical settings: 309 to decide (22 of them are conditional), 1 confirm only) on 50 units. Records: 10 plan decision records, 97 critical setting records, 5 manual action records, 2 plan statement records. Records group four lists: the open decisions of the plans of the draft this run wrote, by the part of the draft (security group, routing, identity, logs, server) and the kind of the decision (plan decisions); the open critical semantics of the units, by the contract family and the semantic (critical semantics); the manual actions of the plans, by the part of the draft and the kind of the action (manual actions); and the open statements of the plans about units they write no resource for (a redesign, a review, a block, a failed model, or a step beside a unit whose draft a converter writes), by the part of the draft and the reason (plan statements). Plan decisions and manual actions cover only drafted units whose draft passed StackToIT's own checks, and only the families whose draft this run wrote from a plan: a family with no plan has none to list. A plan statement covers a unit the plan writes nothing for, whether or not a draft check ran over it; a statement that leaves nothing to a person (a unit the plan does not draft and no manual action of it names) is counted apart from the records and is no record. A record shows the review of an overlay beside the open state the engine reached; a review closes no critical semantic and changes no draft, target plan, gate, class, confidence or eligibility. An accepted plan decision frees the steps of the execution plan that wait for it only when the answer's effect acknowledges the current draft; an option that changes the draft keeps them held until the draft carries that option (the line of the option in decisions-template.yaml says whether an answer of the inputs file writes it or no answer of this build does). The one exception is an option that declines a default of the draft (choose-the-size, choose-the-snapshot-count, choose-the-zone-per-server, keep-the-source-rules-and-redesign-a-firewall, machine-type-with-a-local-disk, persistent-volume-for-the-data): the run that reads that answer writes its draft without the default, and the value the default stood for is yours to set. Records of the family "convert" are decisions of the converter's own generators, outside every plan: a constraint conflict (a variable whose consumers' STACKIT bounds exclude one another keeps the source default) and an ambiguous selection (the source does not prove which instance, interface, key pair, gateway, peer, subnet, proxy, URL map or health check it means, so the draft holds a required variable without a default); the unit that owns one cannot be automated until a person decides. They are listed for a drafted unit whose plan checks did not fail.

Of the 114 records, 1 root blockers (1 open item), 101 open on their own (321 open items), 12 conditional on a count or for_each (26 open items), 0 propagated from a root cause (0 open items). 1 root cause, 0 dependent units. A record is a view over its members: a propagated one stays in the register with every member, it is folded under its root cause below.

A root cause is a unit other open items rest on: the target does not carry its decision, so what the units that name it become is not assessed. Deciding the root is what frees its dependents; each dependent stays a record of its own, folded here.

Accepting a record changes nothing in the draft or in the assessment: the plan's decisions stay open in target-plan.json, an open critical semantic stays open, and the execution plan frees a step that waits for an accepted plan decision only when the answer's effect acknowledges the current draft (an option that changes the draft keeps the step held until the draft is regenerated with it; an option with no stated effect frees nothing); the record shows the architect's answer beside the engine's reading, and no class, confidence, gate or eligibility depends on a record. A record is accepted only when every member it groups is; a partial or outdated approval never makes it accepted, and a rejection is not an approval: a rejected record stays open and is listed under Open as well as under Rejected.

One card per record of the register, the first required action first, then the records you can answer now (those with options to choose from, then those that wait for an input or a confirmation), then the guidance-only records (no choice to make: a check or a person does what they say), in groups by work package: what you do next, what the draft does, what is still open, the ways out and what closes it. What the records of one kind share is said once above them. The record’s own fields (its kind, its units, its options and its review) are folded under Technical details; its owner role and the phase it is required by are on its first line. Under it, each card states its options with the trade-off of each, the applications it touches (a group the run suggested from the source is labelled PROPOSED: it is not an application you confirmed), its wave (the dependency order of the units, a technical order and not a schedule) and where its approval stands (STALE where the answer no longer holds); decisions.json holds every record with its evidence. An answer is recorded in the decisions file given with --decisions, an input in the inputs file given with --inputs; the run folder holds the templates of both files to fill (decisions-template.yaml, inputs-template.yaml). The inputs template has three groups: the requests an answer changes the draft for, the ones a person does by hand, and, last and as comments with no stub, the requests this build records an answer to and does not apply, each with where the setting is made instead (the target environment). No decisions file was given with this run, so no card shows a review.

In the technical details, “None named” under applications of your file means no applications file was given or none of its applications confirmedly contains an affected unit; “None listed” under options means the knowledge base has no options for this kind of decision, so none is invented and a person states the answer in the decisions file; no option is recommended unless its evidence is conclusive (the machine forces no recommendation).

What the draft does
The draft does not carry the setting on module.dependencies.aws_mq_broker.mq. The draft holds TF/stackit_rabbitmq_instance.dependencies_mq, TF/stackit_opensearch_instance.dependencies_catalog_opensearch_this, TF/stackit_mariadb_instance.dependencies_catalog_rds_this, TF/stackit_valkey_instance.dependencies_checkout_elasticache_redis_default and TF/stackit_postgresflex_instance.dependencies_orders_rds_this until this decision is answered by an answer that frees it. The database, cache, search domain, message broker or Kubernetes API is written with its public endpoint and its access list. The step that creates the endpoint waits for this decision.
Still open
That only the clients the source admitted reach the endpoint on the target. The mapping rule for this kind of unit recognises the unit but only passes this setting to a person; it does not decide its value. The broker is either reachable from the public internet or only from private networks.
Ways out
  1. Accept the public endpoint, limited by its access list; needs the client networks that must reach the endpoint, in its access list, the owner's statement that the wider exposure is accepted; effect: The draft is applied as written and the wider exposure is an accepted difference.; risk: Every address the access list admits reaches the endpoint over the internet.
  2. Use the network-area-only scope instead of the public endpoint (Private Preview, on request); needs a STACKIT account enabled for the private preview, and the clients inside the Network Area, for the Kubernetes control plane: the owner's acceptance that the private control plane is not recommended for production and cannot carry the ACL extension, the draft regenerated or changed with the scope before the step is applied; effect: The database or the Kubernetes API is reachable only inside the Network Area. MariaDB, the Key Value Store, OpenSearch and RabbitMQ take no such scope: for them this path is a redesign.; risk: A request of an account that is not enabled is rejected, and the scope of the Kubernetes control plane cannot be changed later. A private preview is not for production: the documentation says it is subject to breaking changes without prior notice.; the draft is generated again with it
  3. Redesign how the clients reach the endpoint; needs a design of the access that neither widens the exposure to an access list nor depends on a private preview the owner has not accepted; effect: A person designs and carries out the access; the drafted step stays held until the design is recorded. Where the service offers no network-area-only scope (MariaDB, Key Value Store, OpenSearch, RabbitMQ, Redis, the Application Load Balancer) this is the only way to a private endpoint.; risk: A redesign needs its own proof; the draft does not carry it.; the draft is generated again with it
What closes it
The knowledge base states no closing condition for a decision of the plan; it is done when an answer in the decisions file accepts the public endpoint with its access list, or when the regenerated draft carries the network-area-only scope or the redesign and the step that creates the endpoint is free. A person sets which networks may reach the STACKIT RabbitMQ instance with its access list (a list of CIDR networks); the draft sets none. Verification: a connection from an address outside the access list is refused by the target endpoint, and one from a client the source admitted is served; the decision is recorded with who decided, its scope and its reason.

Where the source and the target engine differ, the export is converted. The decision offers this option only for a store whose STACKIT service documents a way in with such clients: PostgreSQL Flex, MariaDB (the mysql client loads a dump into an empty instance), SQLServer Flex (a .bak file imported with import_database), Key Value Store (the tutorial migrates a Redis instance by the MIGRATE command) and OpenSearch (the reindex operation). For a store without a documented way in (MongoDB Flex, a memcached cache) it is not offered and the decision offers the tool of the customer's own alone. The source and the target engine may differ (MySQL to MariaDB). The plan holds the steps of this option as typed steps: for a PostgreSQL database, for a MySQL, MariaDB or Aurora MySQL database moving to MariaDB and for an RDS for SQL Server database moving to SQLServer Flex (the native backup, its copy to a STACKIT S3 bucket and the import_database call) the preflight, the rehearsal, the write freeze, the dump or backup and the restore or import inside it, the reconcile and the cleanup; for an ElastiCache, MemoryDB or ElastiCache serverless cache moving to a Key Value Store the preflight, the rehearsal, the write freeze, the copy by a client, the reconcile and the cleanup; for an Amazon Aurora DSQL cluster moving to PostgreSQL Flex the preflight, the rehearsal, the write freeze, the copy of the tables by a client (the schema from the catalogs of the cluster, or from pg_dump --schema-only where the preflight shows that it works, and the rows through the PostgreSQL protocol: no AWS page read documents a dump of a cluster), the reconcile and the cleanup; for an OpenSearch store the write freeze, the copy and the reconcile. For an Aurora DSQL cluster, which has no change stream, this option and the tool of the customer's own are the only ones; the replication of the engine is not offered. For an ElastiCache source, where AWS lists migrate among the commands unavailable for caches running Redis OSS, the copy is a client that iterates the keys with SCAN and copies each with DUMP, PTTL and RESTORE; for a MemoryDB source, where AWS lists migrate, sync, psync, bgsave, save and config among the unavailable commands and the cluster mode is always on, the same client copy runs against every shard primary found with CLUSTER NODES or CLUSTER SLOTS, with TLS where the source has it and an ACL user that reaches every key; whether DUMP, RESTORE and PTTL run on a standard MemoryDB cluster is not stated by AWS, and for a member of a multi-Region cluster, whose page lists PTTL as unsupported, the step says the TTLs are not carried.
  2. Replicate the data with the replication of the source engine until the cutover; effect: A person sets up the replication of the source engine so that the STACKIT instance follows the source while the application keeps writing to the source (for PostgreSQL, logical replication: the schema is copied first with pg_dump --schema-only, a publication on the source and a subscription on the target copy the existing rows and then the changes, and the sequences are copied inside the write freeze because they are not replicated). Only a TCP target group takes the path: a NodePort Service of the draft carries TCP.

Run an Ingress controller on the cluster and put the load balancer in front of it; effect: An Ingress controller (for example ingress-nginx, installed by a Helm release) runs on the SKE cluster and routes the requests by Ingress rules to the ClusterIP Services of the workloads; the load balancer reaches the controller, on the controller's node port at the private IPs of the nodes (the target pool of the draft changed to that port) or through the controller's own Service of type LoadBalancer. Ways out
  1. Place the cluster and the servers in one STACKIT network, and admit the clients of the managed services by access lists naming its range; effect: The Kubernetes cluster is deployed into one network (network.id of stackit_ske_cluster names a STACKIT Network Area network; a node pool states no network, so the tasks the source spread over several subnets share it), the servers are placed in it by their network interfaces (network_id of stackit_network_interface), and a managed database or cache is not placed in a network: its access list (acl of stackit_postgresflex_instance and stackit_mongodbflex_instance) names the range of that network. The other drafted networks of the subnets hold none of these consumers. The draft writes the cluster half of this option by default (network = { id = ... } on the drafted stackit_ske_cluster, marked DEFAULT) where the target project is not stated to be outside a Network Area, the draft asks for no such project, the cluster serves workloads of exactly one drafted network, and every other consumer of that network is placed otherwise (a managed data service has a decision of its own for its access list, a load balancer is placed by the networks of its own block, and a STACKIT File Storage file system takes the client list of its resource pool, ip_acl, and no network id); where one of these does not hold it writes no network.id and a person carries the cluster half out. The access lists of the managed services are a separate default of the draft and not written by this option: a person (or that default) carries the services half out, and the network's step stays held until the decision is answered where the draft binds nothing.
  2. Keep the drafted networks and place each consumer in the network of its tier; effect: A network is kept per source subnet class and each consumer is placed where STACKIT can place it: a server by its network interface, a load balancer by its networks (networks.network_id of stackit_application_load_balancer), the Kubernetes cluster by network.id in one network (its node pools state no network, so one cluster cannot follow a split of its tasks over several networks), and a managed database or cache by an access list naming the range of its tier's network. The draft does not write this placement: a person carries it out, and the network's step stays held.
  3. Redesign the network placement of the workloads; effect: The architect designs the placement outside the draft (for example the cluster in an existing Network Area network of the target environment, or the workloads on servers in the drafted networks); the drafted network is replaced by that design. The draft carries none of it, and the network's step stays held.
  4. Accept that the drafted network holds none of the source's consumers of its subnet; effect: The network is applied as the draft writes it, and none of the consumers the record names is placed in it: the cluster is created without network.id as drafted (which network then holds its nodes is not stated by the sources read), a load balancer takes the network its variable is set to, and a managed database or cache admits the clients of its access list. The source's placement of these workloads in the subnet is not kept; a person accepts that difference, and whether the network's range is still needed is decided with it.

Review the service desired count setting: The mapping rule for this kind of unit recognises the unit but only passes this setting to a person; it does not decide its value. desired_count is the number of tasks ECS keeps running (ecs_service docs: 'Number of instances of the task definition to place and keep running'); on SKE it becomes Deployment replicas or a HorizontalPodAutoscaler floor. The draft writes it as the replicas of the Deployment in kubernetes/<service>/manifests.yaml when it is a literal number (a HorizontalPodAutoscaler owns the count where the service has a scaling target and policy the draft translates; a number that is not visible statically is a REQUIRED_ token) — a person confirms the number. Review the twin ECS service launch type setting: The mapping rule for this kind of unit recognises the unit but only passes this setting to a person; it does not decide its value. aws_ecs_service.launch_type (workload compatibility): the capacity the tasks run on, EC2, FARGATE or EXTERNAL (default EC2; provider docs ecs_service.html.markdown:251), which decides the isolation of a task, its sizing steps and where it can run. Nothing of it is carried: the draft rewrites the service as a Deployment that runs on an SKE node pool and stackit_ske_cluster has no argument for it (the unit names it NOT CARRIED), so a person decides the placement on the target. (knowledge-base evidence, not in this folder) Review the twin ECS task definition cpu setting: The mapping rule for this kind of unit recognises the unit but only passes this setting to a person; it does not decide its value. aws_ecs_task_definition.cpu (workload compatibility) (a facet of the unit): the cpu units reserved for the whole task (required for Fargate). The draft turns it into the cpu request and limit of the container where it writes the manifest; the sizing against the node pools stays a decision. Review the twin ECS task definition memory setting: The mapping rule for this kind of unit recognises the unit but only passes this setting to a person; it does not decide its value. aws_ecs_task_definition.memory (workload compatibility) (a facet of the unit): the memory in MiB reserved for the whole task (required for Fargate). The draft turns it into the memory request and limit of the container where it writes the manifest; the sizing against the node pools stays a decision. Review the twin ECS task definition requires compatibilities setting: The mapping rule for this kind of unit recognises the unit but only passes this setting to a person; it does not decide its value. aws_ecs_task_definition.requires_compatibilities (workload compatibility) (a facet of the unit): the launch types the task is validated against, EC2, EXTERNAL, FARGATE or MANAGED_INSTANCES (provider docs ecs_task_definition.html.markdown:237), which decides where the task can run and which task-level settings are allowed. Nothing of it is carried: the draft rewrites the task as Kubernetes manifests that name the containers, and stackit_ske_cluster has no argument for this task-level setting, so a person chooses the equivalent on the target. The containers of the task: images, commands, environment, secret references, ports, health checks, log configuration - the workload itself, and where its credentials are injected. Decide per container: the image and where it lives, command and entry point, environment, ports and health check, cpu/memory as requests and limits, and the log destination; the secret references and the plaintext secrets among the environment entries are read by the settings of the secret references and of the plaintext secrets, the registry by the setting of the image registry. Confirm the container image registry: The mapping rule for this kind of unit recognises the unit but only passes this setting to a person; it does not decide its value. A container image comes from Amazon ECR (a `.dkr.ecr.` or public.ecr.aws registry host) or needs `repositoryCredentials`. The images are not moved by the draft and a pod on STACKIT cannot assume the ECR pull rights of the ECS execution role. Decide: where the images live on STACKIT (the STACKIT Container Registry has a GA API, the Container Registry API specification, but no Terraform resource in pinned provider; a registry of your choice works too), how they are copied, and the pull secret the cluster uses. Confirm the container plaintext secret env: The mapping rule for this kind of unit recognises the unit but only passes this setting to a person; it does not decide its value. An `environment` entry whose NAME looks like a credential (password, secret, token, api key, private key, credential) carries a non-empty plaintext value in the task definition (a name heuristic, not a proof: the value is never shown). Decide: whether the value is a secret; if it is, it must not be copied into a Kubernetes manifest or a Terraform variable default but stored in a STACKIT Secrets Manager entry and the plaintext copy in the AWS state and task definition rotated. Confirm the container secret references: The mapping rule for this kind of unit recognises the unit but only passes this setting to a person; it does not decide its value. The task definition's container_definitions state secret references (the `secrets` list: name and valueFrom, "the full ARN of the AWS Secrets Manager secret or the full ARN of the parameter in the SSM Parameter Store", AWS ECS API reference, Secret). A person decides first which STACKIT Secrets Manager instance holds each referenced secret (stackit_secretsmanager_instance, pinned provider: name, acls, kms_key; the secret entries themselves have no Terraform resource in the pinned provider, they are created through the API or the portal, and their VALUES are never in the Terraform sources - a person copies them). Second, a person decides how the pods read them (the STACKIT Secrets Manager authenticates with Vault-compatible tokens and AppRole, docs.stackit.cloud/products/security/secrets-manager/; ECS injects valueFrom into environment variables when the container starts, and no STACKIT equivalent of that injection is stated on the documentation page checked 2026-10-06, so the Kubernetes Secret or the in-pod fetch is a design of its own).

Register list (114 records)

One row for each record of the register: 10 plan decision records, 97 critical setting records, 5 manual action records, 2 plan statement records. A row gives the record, what it is about, the units it concerns, its state, why it is open and what answers it, with links to the record’s card, to its units and to its evidence. The rows are listed under one heading for each state and cause, the states that still wait for a person first, so the page needs no script to be read by state or by cause; the index below links to each heading.

The cause of a record is the one the knowledge base gives every item of it (its table of why an item is open, read from typed fields, never from the wording of a message). A record whose items have different causes is listed as mixed causes, and its row names them. “Depends on the unit” means the cause is each unit’s own; “Not classified” means the knowledge base has no entry for the item. Neither is counted as another cause. The state is the review state of the record (the decisions file); a review changes nothing in the draft or in the engine’s reading. Where an answer is an entry of the decisions file, its key is the id of the record.

Customer input
the customer holds the answer: a value or a fact of the running environment, a choice between valid target shapes, or work done outside the tool.
Target limit
STACKIT cannot carry the source behaviour, or its Terraform provider cannot express it: the difference is accepted or an alternative is chosen.
Implementation gap
StackToIT has no reader or generator for something it could carry or check: development work, not a question to the customer.
Depends on the unit
the cause is the unit's own and differs from unit to unit; the page of each unit says which.
Not classified
the knowledge base has no entry that says why this item is open; it is not assigned to any of the other causes.
Mixed causes
the members of the record have different causes; the row lists them.

module.dependencies.aws_security_group.catalog_opensearch_sgsecurity-group-vpc-membershipREVIEWThis draft writes no stackit_security_group, stackit_security_group_rule for this unit: every unit that names the group is a managed data service of STACKIT, which has no security group and takes its clients from an access list of its own, so the group is listed by no resource and what it admitted reaches those access lists as addresses only. What follows states the knowledge base's candidate target, not a block of this draft: Not enforced: the security group is attached to no block of the target (it is written in the draft and listed by no resource, or, where the access lists of its members carry it, not written), so its rules ("security group rules") restrict nothing on the target until an attachment is designed; this setting is not carried as an enforced control. module.vpc.module.vpc.aws_vpc.thisdefault-security-group-omitted-directionREVIEWA check of the knowledge base (vpc default sg no ingress rules) fired on this unit and leaves the setting to a person: the target does not settle it by itself (a finding of this unit describes it). The adopted default security group of the VPC (a facet, aws_default_security_group) does not state an ingress or an egress direction. Nothing is drafted for this facet, so the empty direction is not reproduced: a person decides whether servers that used the default group must stay without outbound traffic (delete the allow-all egress rules of the STACKIT group after apply) or are meant to have it, and puts them in a STACKIT group that states no ingress rule, not in the project's default group.A person decides what this finding asks, and records the evidence or the decision. The finding says: The adopted default security group states no ingress rule. The AWS provider removes every rule of the default group when it adopts it and creates only the stated ones, so after apply the group allows no inbound traffic at all, not even from the members of the group itself. Nothing is drafted for the adopted group: decide which servers relied on the default group and attach them to a STACKIT group that states no ingress rule, not to the project's default group, whose own-member rules would admit its members.a check of the knowledge base (vpc default sg no ingress rules)
